{{Use dmy dates|date=January 2026}}

In [[telecommunication technology]], a '''Barker code''' or '''Barker sequence''' is a finite sequence of digital values with the ideal [[autocorrelation]] property. It is used as a synchronising pattern between the sender and receiver of a stream of bits. Apart from the trivial sequence of length 1, the known Barker sequences have lengths 2, 3, 4, 5, 7, 11 and 13. It is conjectured that no longer sequence exists; this is proved for odd lengths, while the possible existence of an even Barker sequence longer than 4 remains open.<ref name="SW2016">{{cite journal |last1=Schmidt |first1=Kai-Uwe |last2=Willms |first2=Jürgen |title=Barker sequences of odd length |journal=Designs, Codes and Cryptography |volume=80 |issue=2 |pages=409–414 |year=2016 |doi=10.1007/s10623-015-0104-4}}</ref><ref name="Willms2021">{{cite arXiv |last=Willms |first=Jürgen |title=A note on Barker sequences of even length |eprint=2104.00502 |class=math.CO |year=2021}}</ref>

==Explanation==
A stream of [[binary digits]] carries no timing information by itself: the receiver cannot tell where one group of digits ends and the next begins. Transmitting a pre-arranged pattern of digits resolves this, provided the receiver can recognise that pattern reliably. In simple terms it is equivalent to attaching a label to one digit, after which the positions of the remaining digits follow by counting.

Such a pattern is useful only if it is unlikely to be imitated by the surrounding data or by noise, and if a partial overlap between the received signal and the stored pattern gives a much weaker response than exact alignment. The relevant measure is the pattern's [[autocorrelation]]: the correlation of the pattern with a shifted copy of itself should be large at zero shift and small at every other shift, so that a correlator or [[matched filter]] in the receiver produces a sharp, unambiguous indication of the correct position. Barker sequences are the binary patterns for which these off-peak values are as small as possible; they are named after [[Ronald Hugh Barker]], who set out this requirement for group synchronisation in 1953.<ref name="Barker 1953 pp273–287">{{cite book |last=Barker |first=Ronald Hugh |author-link=Ronald Hugh Barker |date=1953 |title=Communication Theory |place=London |publisher=Butterworth |chapter=Group Synchronizing of Binary Digital Systems |pages=273–287 }}</ref>

==Origins and historical development==
Barker sequences originate in the problem of ''group synchronisation'' in early digital communication systems: a receiver presented with a continuous stream of binary digits must establish where each group of digits begins, and does so by recognising a pre-arranged pattern inserted into the stream. In a 1953 chapter on the group synchronising of binary digital systems, [[Ronald Hugh Barker]] argued that such a pattern should have an autocorrelation function with very low off-peak values, so that it can be recognised unambiguously by the detector and is unlikely to be imitated by a random series of noise-generated bits.<ref name="Barker 1953 pp273–287" /><ref name="Siegel 1971">{{cite thesis |last=Siegel |first=Irv D. |date=1971 |title=Development of a Set of Optimum Synchronisation Codes for a Unique Decoder Mechanization |url=https://scholarsmine.mst.edu/masters_theses/5479 |degree=Masters |publisher=Missouri S & T Library and Learning Resources |page=13 |access-date=5 February 2023 }}</ref>

Binary patterns with low off-peak autocorrelation proved useful both for synchronisation in [[data transmission]] and [[telemetry]] and, as binary phase codes, for [[pulse compression]] in radar. The question of which lengths admit such patterns was subsequently recast as a problem about binary sequences, cyclic difference sets and character sums, and was taken up by [[Richard Turyn]], James Storer and later authors.<ref name="TS1961">{{cite journal |last1=Turyn |first1=Richard J. |last2=Storer |first2=James |title=On binary sequences |journal=Proceedings of the American Mathematical Society |volume=12 |issue=3 |pages=394–399 |year=1961 |doi=10.1090/S0002-9939-1961-0125026-2}}</ref>

==Definition==
[[File:Barker7code.svg|thumb|Graphical representation of a Barker-7 code]]
[[File:Barker7corr.svg|thumb|[[Autocorrelation]] function of a Barker-7 code]]
[[File:3D Doppler Radar Spectrum showing a Barker Code of 13.jpg|thumb|3D [[Doppler radar]] spectrum showing a Barker code of 13]]

A '''Barker code''' or '''Barker sequence''' is a finite sequence of ''N'' values of +1 and &minus;1,

:<math>a_j \text{ for } j = 1, 2, \dots, N</math>

with the ideal autocorrelation property, such that the off-peak (non-cyclic) autocorrelation coefficients

:<math>c_v = \sum_{j=1}^{N-v} a_j a_{j+v} </math>

are as small as possible:

:<math>|c_v| \le 1\,</math>

for all <math>1 \le v < N</math>.<ref name="Barker 1953 pp273–287" />

Apart from the trivial sequence of length 1, nine Barker sequences are known when sequences are identified up to negation and reversal, all of length ''N'' at most 13.<ref>{{Cite OEIS |1=A091704 }}</ref> A stricter equivalence that also identifies sequences related by alternating sign changes reduces this to seven representatives.<ref name="BM">{{cite book |title=Number Theory and Polynomials |editor=James McKee |editor2=Chris Smyth |publisher=Cambridge University Press |isbn=978-0-521-71467-9 |series=LMS Lecture Notes |volume=352 |date=2008 |first1=Peter |last1=Borwein |author-link1=Peter Borwein |first2=Michael J. |last2=Mossinghoff |chapter=Barker sequences and flat polynomials |pages=71–88 |doi=10.1017/CBO9780511721274.007 }}</ref> [[Ronald Hugh Barker|Barker]]'s 1953 chapter instead imposed the stronger, one-sided condition
:<math>c_v \in \{-1, 0\}.</math>
Only four of the known sequences satisfy this stricter condition; these are shown in bold in the table below.<ref name="BM" />

Since <math>c_0 = N</math> trivially, and for <math>v > 0</math> the sum <math>c_v</math> consists of <math>N-v</math> terms each equal to +1 or &minus;1, it follows that <math>c_v \equiv N-v \pmod 2</math>. Consequently the smallest value <math>|c_v|</math> can take is 0 when <math>N-v</math> is even and 1 when <math>N-v</math> is odd; a Barker sequence attains this minimum at every nonzero shift.<ref name="SchmidtCorrelation">{{cite journal |last=Schmidt |first=Kai-Uwe |title=Sequences with small correlation |journal=Designs, Codes and Cryptography |volume=78 |issue=1 |pages=237–267 |year=2016 |doi=10.1007/s10623-015-0154-7 |arxiv=1602.03722}}</ref> The Barker property is unaffected by negating every term, by reversing the sequence, and (up to a sign change in <math>c_v</math>) by alternating negation <math>a_j \mapsto (-1)^j a_j</math>; sequences related by these operations are usually treated as equivalent.<ref name="BM" />

Barker codes of length ''N'' equal to 11 and 13 are used in [[direct-sequence spread spectrum]]  and [[pulse compression|pulse compression radar]] systems because of their low autocorrelation properties (the sidelobe level of amplitude of the Barker codes is 1/''N'' that of the peak signal).<ref name="Skolnik" /> A Barker code resembles a discrete version of a continuous [[chirp]], another low-autocorrelation signal used in other pulse compression radars.

The positive and negative amplitudes of the pulses forming the Barker codes imply the use of biphase modulation or binary [[phase-shift keying]]; that is, the [[phase shifting|change of phase]] in the [[carrier wave]] is 180 degrees.

Similar to the Barker codes are the [[complementary sequence]]s, which cancel sidelobes exactly when summed; the even-length Barker code pairs are also complementary pairs.  There is a simple constructive method to create arbitrarily long complementary sequences.

For the case of cyclic autocorrelation, other sequences have the same property of having perfect (and uniform) sidelobes, such as prime-length [[Legendre symbol|Legendre sequences]], [[Zadoff–Chu sequence]]s (used in 3rd- and 4th-generation cellular radio) and <math>2^n - 1</math> [[maximum length sequence]]s (MLS). Arbitrarily long cyclic sequences can be constructed.

==Barker sequence conjecture==
{{unsolved|mathematics|Does there exist a Barker sequence of length greater than 13? Equivalently, does one exist of even length greater than 4?}}
The '''Barker sequence conjecture''', often attributed to [[Richard Turyn]], states that no Barker sequence has length greater than 13.<ref name="SW2016" /><ref name="BM" /> The odd-length case has been settled; the remaining question is whether an even Barker sequence of length greater than 4 exists.<ref name="Willms2021" />

===Odd lengths===
Turyn and Storer concluded in 1961 that, apart from the trivial length-1 case, an odd-length Barker sequence must have

:<math>N\in\{3,5,7,11,13\}.</math><ref name="TS1961" />

In 2014, Jürgen Willms exhibited counterexamples to an intermediate theorem used in their published proof, showing that the proof as written was incomplete.<ref name="WillmsCorrection">{{cite arXiv |last=Willms |first=Jürgen |title=Counterexamples to Theorem 1 of Turyn's and Storer's paper “On Binary Sequences” |eprint=1404.4833 |class=math.NT |year=2014}}</ref> The classification itself remains valid: Peter Borwein and Tamás Erdélyi gave a different proof using Barker polynomials, and Schmidt and Willms later gave a new proof.<ref name="BE2013">{{cite journal |last1=Borwein |first1=Peter |last2=Erdélyi |first2=Tamás |title=A note on Barker polynomials |journal=International Journal of Number Theory |volume=9 |issue=3 |pages=759–767 |year=2013 |doi=10.1142/S179304211250159X |arxiv=1206.5371}}</ref><ref name="SW2016" />

===Even lengths and exclusion bounds===
A hypothetical even Barker sequence of length <math>N>4</math> must have

:<math>N=4u^2</math>

for an odd integer <math>u</math>, and the prime divisors of <math>u</math> must satisfy further number-theoretic restrictions.<ref name="Turyn1965">{{cite journal |last=Turyn |first=Richard J. |title=Character sums and difference sets |journal=Pacific Journal of Mathematics |volume=15 |issue=1 |pages=319–346 |year=1965 |doi=10.2140/pjm.1965.15.319}}</ref><ref name="LS2016">{{cite journal |last1=Leung |first1=Ka Hin |last2=Schmidt |first2=Bernhard |title=The anti-field-descent method |journal=Journal of Combinatorial Theory, Series A |volume=139 |pages=87–131 |year=2016 |doi=10.1016/j.jcta.2015.11.005}}</ref>

Successive field-descent and computational results have pushed the rigorous exclusion range far beyond the lengths accessible by direct enumeration. Bernhard Schmidt excluded <math>13<N<4\times10^{12}</math> in 2002,<ref name="Schmidt2002">{{cite book |last=Schmidt |first=Bernhard |title=Characters and Cyclotomic Fields in Finite Geometry |series=Lecture Notes in Mathematics |volume=1797 |publisher=Springer |year=2002 |isbn=978-3-540-44243-1 |doi=10.1007/b84213}}</ref> and Leung and Schmidt extended this to <math>13<N<10^{22}</math> in 2005.<ref name="LS2005">{{cite journal |last1=Leung |first1=Ka Hin |last2=Schmidt |first2=Bernhard |title=The field descent method |journal=Designs, Codes and Cryptography |volume=36 |issue=2 |pages=171–188 |year=2005 |doi=10.1007/s10623-004-1703-7}}</ref> In 2014, Borwein and Mossinghoff showed that a Barker sequence longer than 13 would have either

:<math>N=3\,979\,201\,339\,721\,749\,133\,016\,171\,583\,224\,100</math>

or <math>N>4\times10^{33}</math>.<ref name="BM2014">{{cite journal |last1=Borwein |first1=Peter |last2=Mossinghoff |first2=Michael J. |title=Wieferich pairs and Barker sequences, II |journal=LMS Journal of Computation and Mathematics |volume=17 |issue=1 |pages=24–32 |year=2014 |doi=10.1112/S1461157013000223 |arxiv=1306.0045}}</ref> Leung and Schmidt subsequently eliminated the exceptional value, proving that no Barker sequence exists for <math>13<N\leq4\times10^{33}</math>.<ref name="LS2016" />

Logan and Mossinghoff reported in 2017 that the smallest ''known'' integer surviving all restrictions they tested was <math>N=4u^2</math>, where

:<math>u=19\,804\,304\,830\,012\,264\,298\,738\,041,</math>

so that <math>N\approx1.57\times10^{51}</math>. They noted, however, that their enumeration was complete only over a smaller parameter range, so this is not a rigorous improvement of the <math>4\times10^{33}</math> exclusion bound.<ref name="LoganMossinghoff2017">{{cite journal |last1=Logan |first1=Brooke |last2=Mossinghoff |first2=Michael J. |title=Double Wieferich pairs and circulant Hadamard matrices |journal=Journal of Combinatorial Mathematics and Combinatorial Computing |volume=101 |pages=145–156 |year=2017 |url=https://combinatorialpress.com/jcmcc-articles/volume-101/double-wieferich-pairs-and-circulant-hadamard-matrices/ |access-date=5 August 2026}}</ref>

A 2021 preprint by Willms derived a form of weak symmetry for a hypothetical even Barker sequence and proved that none of length <math>N>4</math> can satisfy

:<math>c_1=c_3=\cdots=c_{N/2-1}.</math>

This excludes a special pattern of odd-shift correlations but does not settle the general even-length case.<ref name="Willms2021" />

===Relation to circulant Hadamard matrices===
For a sequence of length <math>N</math>, its periodic autocorrelation at shift <math>v</math> is <math>r_v=c_v+c_{N-v}</math>. If a Barker sequence has even length <math>N>2</math>, then <math>r_v=0</math> at every nonzero shift. The circulant matrix whose first row is the sequence therefore has mutually orthogonal rows and is a [[circulant Hadamard matrix]] of order <math>N</math>.<ref name="SchmidtCorrelation" /><ref name="LS2016" />

[[Ryser's conjecture on circulant Hadamard matrices]] states that no circulant Hadamard matrix has order greater than 4. It would therefore imply the Barker sequence conjecture. The implication is one-way: the circulant Hadamard condition controls the sums <math>c_v+c_{N-v}</math>, whereas the Barker condition separately requires <math>|c_v|\leq1</math>.<ref name="SchmidtCorrelation" />

===Polynomial formulation===
To a Barker sequence one may associate the [[Littlewood polynomial]]

:<math>P(z)=\sum_{j=1}^{N}a_jz^{j-1}.</math>

Its autocorrelations occur as the coefficients in

:<math>P(z)P(z^{-1})=N+\sum_{v=1}^{N-1}c_v(z^v+z^{-v}).</math>

This formulation connects Barker sequences with flat-polynomial problems, Mahler measure and norms of Littlewood polynomials.<ref name="BM" /> Gang Yu obtained improved estimates in 2023 for the <math>L^1</math>-norms of Barker polynomials and, more generally, Littlewood polynomials; the estimates do not resolve the conjecture.<ref name="Yu2023">{{cite journal |last=Yu |first=Gang |title=A Note on Barker Sequences and the L1-norm of Littlewood Polynomials |journal=Comptes Rendus Mathématique |volume=361 |pages=609–616 |year=2023 |doi=10.5802/crmath.428|doi-access=free }}</ref>

==Implementation in communication systems==
[[File:BarkerMod-BPSK.jpg|thumb|A Barker code transmitted using [[BPSK|binary phase-shift keying]]]]

A Barker sequence is a code or spreading sequence rather than a modulation scheme in its own right; its symbols are normally transmitted using binary phase modulation, with <math>+1</math> and <math>-1</math> represented by carrier phases differing by <math>\pi</math> radians (180 degrees), that is, by [[phase-shift keying|binary phase-shift keying]].

In wireless systems, spreading and synchronisation sequences are chosen for their autocorrelation properties, for low cross correlation with other sequences likely to interfere, and for their spectral characteristics. The legacy [[direct-sequence spread spectrum]] modes of [[IEEE 802.11b]] use the length-11 Barker sequence for the 1 and 2&nbsp;Mbit/s data rates.<ref name="KeysightWLAN">{{Cite web |url=http://literature.cdn.keysight.com/litweb/pdf/5988-3762EN.pdf |title=RF Testing of WLAN Products |website=Keysight Technologies }}</ref> With the sign convention used there, the aperiodic autocorrelation of that particular sequence takes the value +11 at zero shift and 0 or &minus;1 at every other shift.<ref name="KeysightWLAN" />

== Applications ==

=== Established applications ===
Barker sequences are used as synchronisation patterns in digital communication and [[telemetry]] systems: a correlator or matched filter detects the known pattern in the received bit stream and thereby establishes group, frame or symbol timing.<ref name="Barker 1953 pp273–287" /><ref name="Siegel 1971" />

They are also used as short binary phase codes for [[pulse compression]] in [[radar]] and sonar. Because the aperiodic autocorrelation of a Barker sequence of length ''N'' has a peak of ''N'' and off-peak values of magnitude at most 1, matched filtering gives fine range resolution while keeping range sidelobes low.<ref name="Skolnik">{{cite book |last=Skolnik |first=Merrill I. |title=Introduction to Radar Systems |edition=3rd |publisher=McGraw-Hill |year=2001 |isbn=978-0-07-290980-7}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Majid |first=Alolaibi |date=2021 |title=Low noise moving target detection in high resolution radar using binary code |journal=EURASIP Journal on Advances in Signal Processing |volume=2021 |issue=1 |article-number=8 |bibcode=2021EJASP2021....8A |doi=10.1186/s13634-020-00716-0 |doi-access=free }}</ref>

In [[Wi-Fi]], the length-11 Barker sequence was standardised for the direct-sequence 1 and 2&nbsp;Mbit/s modes of [[IEEE 802.11b]]; the 5.5 and 11&nbsp;Mbit/s modes use [[complementary code keying]] instead.<ref name="KeysightWLAN" /><ref>{{Cite book |last1=Mikulka |first1=Jan |last2=Hanus |first2=Stanislav |date=2007 |title=2007 17th International Conference Radioelektronika |chapter=CCK and Barker Coding Implementation in IEEE 802.11b Standard |pages=1–4 |doi=10.1109/RADIOELEK.2007.371484 |s2cid=34865532 }}</ref>

=== Other studied applications ===
Barker-coded excitation has been investigated for [[ultrasound]] imaging and for ultrasonic nondestructive testing, where coding the transmitted pulse improves the signal-to-noise ratio available at low drive voltages.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Zhao |first1=Heng |last2=L. Mo |first2=Larry |last3=Gao |first3=Shangkai |date=2007 |title=Barker-Coded Ultrasound Color Flow Imaging: Theoretical and practical design considerations |journal=IEEE Transactions on Ultrasonics, Ferroelectrics and Frequency Control |volume=54 |issue=2 |pages=319–331 |doi=10.1109/tuffc.2007.246 |pmid=17328329 |bibcode=2007ITUFF..54..319Z |s2cid=19527352}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Fan |first1=Zeng |last2=Rudlin |first2=Ohn |last3=Asfis |first3=Giorgos |last4=Meng |first4=Hongying |date=2019 |title=Convolution of Barker and Golay Codes for Low Voltage Ultrasonic Testing |journal=Technologies |volume=7 |issue=4 |page=72 |doi=10.3390/technologies7040072 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

Barker sequences have also appeared in individual designs and experimental systems. Reported examples include a digital modulator and demodulator for [[RFID]] tags using direct-sequence spread spectrum with Barker coding,<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Amin |first1=Syedul |last2=Reaz |first2=Mamun Bin Ibne |last3=Jalil |first3=Jubayer |last4=Raham |first4=LF |date=2012 |title=Digital Modulator and Demodulator IC for RFID Tag Employing DSSS and Barker Code |journal=Journal of Applied Research and Technology |volume=10 |issue=6 |pages=819–825 |doi=10.22201/ICAT.16656423.2012.10.6.341 |s2cid=16796254 |doi-access=free}}</ref> codes formed by concatenating Barker sequences with nonlinear feedback shift register sequences,<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Matsuyuki |first1=Shota |last2=Tsuneda |first2=Akio |date=2018 |title=2018 International Conference on Information and Communication Technology Convergence (ICTC) |chapter=A Study on Aperiodic Auto-Correlation Properties of Concatenated Codes by Barker Sequences and NFSR Sequences |isbn=978-1-5386-5041-7 |pages=664–666 |doi=10.1109/ICTC.2018.8539367 |s2cid=53713772}}</ref> a proposed scheme combining Barker codes with binary complements with the stated aim of improving the security of spread-spectrum transmissions,<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Latif |first1=Shahid |last2=Kamran |first2=Muhammad |last3=Masoud |first3=Fahad |last4=Sohaib |first4=Muhammad |date=2012 |title=2012 International Conference on Emerging Technologies |chapter=Improving DSSS transmission security using Barker code along binary compliments (CBC12-DSSS) |isbn=978-1-4673-4451-7 |pages=1–5 |doi=10.1109/ICET.2012.6375426 |s2cid=2901603}}</ref> and joint radar-and-communication waveforms studied for automotive and [[Intelligent Transport Systems|intelligent transport]] use.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Bekar |first1=Muge |last2=Baker |first2=Chris |last3=Hoare |first3=Edward |last4=Gashinova |first4=Marina |date=2021 |title=Joint MIMO Radar and Communication System Using a PSK-LFM Waveform With TDM and CDM Approaches |journal=IEEE Sensors Journal |volume=21 |issue=5 |pages=6115–6124 |bibcode=2021ISenJ..21.6115B |doi=10.1109/JSEN.2020.3043085 |s2cid=231852192 |doi-access=free}}</ref> These are particular implementations or research proposals; they do not by themselves establish widespread deployment.
